title: Bruke det i væresetninger — using det in weather sentences
goal: Use fixed det when weather or ambient predication has no semantic subject.

objectives.statement: Use fixed det when weather or ambient predication has no semantic subject.

spans.value: Mina and Jonas are preparing to meet outside a café in Bergen. Mina is already on her way, but the weather is getting worse.
Hei, Jonas. Er du på vei?

blocks.translation: Hi, Jonas. Are you on your way?

spans.value: Ikke ennå. Hvordan er været der?

blocks.translation: Not yet. What is the weather like there?

spans.value: Det regner, og det blåser ganske mye.

blocks.translation: It’s raining, and it’s quite windy.

spans.value: Å nei. Er det kaldt også?

blocks.translation: Oh no. Is it cold too?

spans.value: Ja, det er kaldt, og det begynner å bli mørkt.

blocks.translation: Yes, it’s cold, and it’s starting to get dark.

spans.value: Da møtes vi inne på kafeen.

blocks.translation: Then we’ll meet inside the café.

spans.value: God idé. Det er varmt og hyggelig der inne.

blocks.translation: Good idea. It’s warm and pleasant inside.

spans.value: does not identify a particular object. Mina is not saying that some object called “it” is raining, cold, or dark. Norwegian requires a grammatical subject in these statements, so it uses fixed
when weather or an ambient condition has no real person or thing performing the action or possessing the quality.
English also commonly uses “it” in weather expressions:
in much the same way. This use is often called a dummy subject or formal subject. You do not need to analyze that label when speaking. The practical point is simple:

statement.value: When you describe weather or a general condition and there is no actual person or thing to use as the subject, begin the statement with fixed

spans.value: The important choice is not whether English happens to include the word “it” in every translation. The important choice is whether Norwegian needs a subject even though no particular person or thing is being described.

sections.title: Transfer: a morning at the cabin

spans.value: The next weekend, Jonas is staying at a cabin. Mina asks whether they can go for a walk. Conditions are different from the café scene: it is snowing, the cabin is warm, and daylight is beginning to fade.

explanation.value: Mina: «Det regner, og det blåser ganske mye.» Mina: «Det er kaldt, og det begynner å bli mørkt.»

options.text: «Det» refers to a particular thing called været.
options.why: No particular thing is being described; the sentences report weather and surrounding conditions.

options.text: «Det» is fixed only before regner and blåser.
options.why: The clauses with er and blir also describe conditions without a named semantic subject.

options.text: «Det» fills the subject position without naming a particular thing.
options.why: Norwegian uses fixed «det» in weather and ambient clauses that have no semantic subject.

stem.value: Mina: «Det regner, og det blåser ganske mye.» Mina: «Det er kaldt, og det begynner å bli mørkt.»

explanation.value: Værverbene regner, snør og blåser står direkte etter det faste «det». Vi setter ikke inn «er».

prompt.value: Sort the sentences by what they describe.

explanation.value: «Er» beskriver en tilstand nå, mens «blir» beskriver en forandring.

options.why: The second sentence presents darkness as a state rather than a change in progress.

options.text: Det blir lyst klokka 15. Det blir mørkt klokka 17.

prompt.value: Lea writes: «Hei! Hvordan er været i Bergen i dag? Kan vi spise ute?» Notes: rain, low temperature, outdoor seating closed. Reply to Lea so she can decide where to eat. Write the weather and condition details in a natural way.

payload.judge_prompt: Judge only the visible reply task using criteria reply-to-lea, fixed-det, supplied-facts.

criteria.instruction: Writes a coherent Norwegian reply to Lea that helps her decide where to eat.
Weather and ambient clauses in the reply use fixed «det».
Reports all three facts: it is raining, it is cold, and the café terrace is closed.

payload.feedback: A weather statement needs fixed «det» when no subject is already present: «Ja, det regner fortsatt, og det blåser mer enn før.» A coordinated verb can share that subject.

prompt.value: Mina asks if you can go for a walk now. Cabin note: snow and low temperature outside; warm inside; it will be dark soon. Write Mina a message with these details, and say whether you should go now or wait. Use common weather and condition phrases, and describe it getting dark as a change.

payload.judge_prompt: Judge only the visible message task using criteria message-to-mina, all-cabin-facts, fixed-det, change-form, recommendation.

criteria.instruction: Writes a coherent Norwegian message to Mina about the proposed walk.
Reports all four facts: it is snowing outside, it is cold outside, it is warm inside, and the daylight is fading or it is getting dark.
Weather and ambient clauses in the message use fixed «det».
The fading daylight is expressed as a changing condition with «blir».
Recommends either going now or waiting.

prompt.value: Mina is writing to Jonas from Bergen. Note: rain and low temperature. Write a natural message. Use one sentence about the weather and one sentence about the conditions.

payload.judge_prompt: Judge the correction using criteria two-correct-clauses. A valid variant that must pass is «Det regner i Bergen, og det er kaldt ute.» A near-miss that must fail is «Det er regner i Bergen, og det er kaldt.» because the rain clause still has the wrong form «er regner»; the cold clause «det er kaldt» is itself correct.

criteria.instruction: The corrected message has a complete rain clause with fixed «det» and no «er», and a complete cold ambient clause with the neuter form «kaldt».

explanation.value: Et værverb står direkte etter det faste «det», uten «er».
